description: We confront complexity with discipline, order chaos through knowledge, and accept the responsibility to solve what others leave unexplained.
summary: Deep Field turns NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey into something anyone can watch. Type any name or coordinates and it builds that patch of sky from NASA’s archive, then plays every SPHEREx visit as a short film, so anything that moves or flickers stands out. It doesn’t just show change, it measures it. For fast-moving stars, it fits each visit’s position to a fraction of a pixel and calculates the star’s motion with an error bar. Our measurement of Barnard’s Star, 10.39 ± 0.54 arcseconds per year, matches ESA’s Gaia (10.39), and a star that shouldn’t move measures as zero. Click any point to see its spectrum across SPHEREx’s 102 colours, or let the tool find what changed automatically. When the data can’t support an answer, for example a saturated or blended star, it says so instead of guessing. A Simple view serves the public and citizen scientists; a Pro view serves astronomers.
details:
What it does: Deep Field answers the SPHEREx challenge, “type a position, see that sky as a video.” Enter any name or coordinates and the app searches NASA’s IRSA archive, downloads SPHEREx cutouts, aligns them on a common grid and plays each visit as a frame. Five challenge targets open instantly; new positions take a few minutes the first time, then load instantly.

How it works: For each visit we subtract the background, combine exposures weighted by noise and fit a 2D Gaussian to find the star’s position to a fraction of a pixel. A straight-line fit through time gives the motion, with error bars inflated whenever the data scatters more than expected. Spectra are built on click from every exposure, since each one sees a different wavelength. “Find what changed” scores every pixel against a smooth, unchanging model and flags outliers. No trained AI model is used for the science.

Validation: Every measurement is graded against ESA’s Gaia DR3, which is never an input. Barnard’s Star agrees to within 0.1σ and ε Indi Ba to within 0.5σ, and RW Aurigae, our control star, shows no motion. The Proof page documents every method with its maths and code, plus the bugs real data caught: https://deep-field-theta.vercel.app/proof

Impact: Citizen scientists, such as Backyard Worlds volunteers, already hunt moving stars by flipping through images by hand. Deep Field gives them SPHEREx in a browser, including on a phone, while the Pro workstation gives astronomers layers, a timeline, spectra and full processing details.

Honesty and limits: The tool refuses rather than guesses on saturated or blended sources. Known limits: parallax isn’t modelled, and brown dwarfs need better spectral templates. The experimental Planet X pages use simulated data and are labelled that way throughout.

Tools: Python (Astropy, NumPy, SciPy), FastAPI, Next.js/React, Aladin Lite. Hosted on Vercel. Code: https://github.com/zenith600/spaceapps2026_team_-Helios
